phases.name: Define the enforcement contract
phases.description: Keep the supplied rate-limit brief visible, state provisional identity and policy assumptions, and add the existing catalog components for the request, decision, state, and operations paths.

phases.name: Connect the synchronous request path
phases.description: Route callers through the gateway, check shared state and policy, forward only allowed requests, and return a useful limit response at the API boundary.

phases.name: Observe breaches asynchronously
phases.description: Send bounded breach telemetry off the request path, aggregate it, and alert from operational signals.

phases.name: Review algorithm, accuracy, and scale tradeoffs
phases.description: Choose a default algorithm while preserving policy-level alternatives, address clock and state-store behavior, and scale from measured hot spots and latency.

steps.title: Read the frozen brief and label assumptions
steps.content: The frozen problem is Design an API Rate Limiter: Design a rate limiting system to control the number of requests a user can make to an API. Requirements are: Limit requests per user/IP within time window; Support different rate limit tiers; Provide clear error messages when limit exceeded; Track and reset limits per time window; Support distributed rate limiting; Monitor and alert on rate limit breaches; Handle millions of requests per second. Constraints are: Low latency overhead (<10ms); Accurate counting in distributed system; Handle clock skew across servers; Memory efficient implementation; Support multiple rate limit algorithms. Hints are token bucket or leaky bucket, Redis for distributed counters, sliding window log or fixed window counter, in-memory cache for performance, and rate limit headers. Treat hints as options. Provisional assumptions to review: authenticated requests use the validated principal as their subject; anonymous requests use a normalized client IP obtained through trusted proxy metadata; versioned tier policies are configured outside the request path; and one authoritative Redis partition owns each subject's counter decisions. The brief supplies no tier values, window lengths, regional topology, state-store failure posture, or consistency allowance between regions. Do not turn these unknowns into numeric service promises.

steps.title: Add an API caller
steps.content: Use this existing Web App as a representative API consumer. Other clients use the same public request and response contract; the limiter keys decisions from validated identity or trusted client network metadata rather than trusting a caller-supplied forwarding header.

component.label: API Client
component.description: Representative consumer of the rate-limited API

properties.purpose: Call the public API with its authenticated identity when available; display the documented rate-limit error and retry guidance without attempting to override trusted client identity metadata.

component.highlightReason: The existing Web App catalog component represents a caller without inventing a client-specific component type.

steps.title: Distribute ingress traffic
steps.content: Spread requests across gateway instances and perform health-aware routing. The balancer is not the authoritative limiter: sticky routing alone would allow a caller's state to split across gateway instances.

component.label: API Ingress Load Balancer
component.description: Health-aware routing to API gateway instances

properties.purpose: Distribute API requests across healthy gateway instances while preserving trusted client address metadata; do not rely on instance affinity for rate-limit correctness.

component.highlightReason: The existing Load Balancer catalog item covers ingress distribution and health-aware routing.

steps.title: Enforce limits at the API gateway
steps.content: Validate the request identity, resolve the applicable subject and tier policy, evaluate the selected algorithm, and forward only allowed requests. On denial, return HTTP 429 with a stable error code and message plus RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, RateLimit-Reset, and Retry-After where the selected algorithm can provide them.

component.label: Rate-Limiting API Gateway
component.description: Identity-aware policy evaluation and API throttling boundary

properties.purpose: Validate JWT identity and trusted client metadata, resolve versioned tier policy from a bounded local policy cache, run the configured rate-limit algorithm against shared state, and route only allowed calls to the application. Return actionable HTTP 429 errors with limit, remaining, reset, and retry guidance when available; never treat a local counter as the globally authoritative count.

component.highlightReason: The existing API Gateway catalog component already exposes authentication, rateLimiting, and throttling properties; no custom limiter component is needed.

steps.title: Add shared Redis counter state
steps.content: Keep the decision state shared across gateway instances. An atomic server-side operation reads and updates the subject's selected policy state together; expiry follows that algorithm's window or idle-refill semantics so inactive keys can be reclaimed without silently splitting live counts across local caches.

component.label: Redis Rate-Limit State
component.description: Atomic distributed counters and compact algorithm state

properties.purpose: Hold compact per-subject and per-policy counter or token state shared by gateway instances; apply check-and-update atomically on the authoritative shard, use datastore time for window/refill decisions, and expire state according to policy semantics. This is correctness state, not an independently incremented local cache.

component.highlightReason: The existing Cache catalog item supports Redis and in-memory storage, which represent the hinted shared counter store without a custom component.

steps.title: Store versioned tier policies
steps.content: Keep policy configuration separate from hot request counters. A policy identifies its subject scope, tier, algorithm, window or refill behavior, response guidance, and policy version; the brief defines none of the tier values, so leave them as configuration rather than inventing quotas.

component.label: Rate-Limit Policy Store
component.description: Versioned per-tier algorithm and window configuration

properties.purpose: Persist versioned policies for user and IP scopes, tier selection, supported algorithm, window or refill semantics, and client response guidance; publish policy changes so gateways can refresh their bounded local policy cache. Do not store per-request hot counters here.

component.highlightReason: The existing Database catalog item represents durable policy configuration; the concept does not require a custom component.

steps.title: Protect the application service
steps.content: Keep business handling behind the gateway. Rejected calls stop before this service; allowed calls continue with the validated identity and applicable policy context where the application needs it.

component.label: Protected API Service
component.description: Business API reached only after gateway admission

properties.purpose: Handle business API requests only after the gateway admits them; keep rate-limit enforcement at the shared ingress boundary so calls cannot bypass the policy by reaching an application instance directly.

component.highlightReason: The existing Backend Server catalog component represents the protected application without introducing a rate-limiter-specific type.

steps.title: Buffer breach telemetry off the hot path
steps.content: Export bounded, privacy-safe breach and evaluation telemetry asynchronously. Aggregate or batch repetitive denials instead of blocking a user request on an individual event write or emitting raw credentials and untrusted identity headers.

component.label: Rate-Limit Telemetry Queue
component.description: Asynchronous transport for aggregated breach signals

properties.purpose: Buffer privacy-safe, aggregated limit denials and evaluation health signals for downstream monitoring; keep publication asynchronous and define bounded retry and retention behavior so telemetry backpressure does not add request-path latency.

component.highlightReason: The existing Queue catalog item can carry operational events without adding a custom telemetry component.

steps.title: Aggregate operational signals
steps.content: Aggregate accepted and denied decisions, evaluation latency, datastore errors, policy versions, and memory/key-cardinality signals by safe dimensions such as route and tier. Avoid cardinality explosions from raw subject identifiers.

component.label: Rate-Limit Metrics Aggregator
component.description: Aggregate denial, latency, state-store, and capacity signals

properties.purpose: Consume batched rate-limit telemetry and aggregate breach volume, allow/deny outcomes, evaluation latency, Redis errors, policy-version skew, and state cardinality by bounded operational dimensions; exclude raw credentials and avoid per-subject metric labels.

component.highlightReason: The existing Analytics catalog item covers metrics aggregation using supported catalog properties.

steps.title: Alert on breaches and limiter health
steps.content: Alert on sustained breach patterns and on failures that can invalidate enforcement, including elevated evaluation latency, datastore errors, memory pressure, key growth, policy propagation delay, and observed clock drift. Set alert thresholds from operating evidence because the brief supplies no alert thresholds.

component.label: Rate-Limit Monitoring and Alerts

properties.purpose: Monitor aggregated breach patterns, request evaluation latency, Redis errors and memory pressure, policy propagation delay, and clock drift; route actionable alerts to operators without labeling raw user or IP identifiers.

component.highlightReason: The existing Monitoring catalog item explicitly supports metrics and alerts for this operational requirement.

steps.title: Route the caller to ingress
steps.content: Send the consumer request to the health-aware public ingress. Preserve only trusted network metadata for anonymous IP-based policies.

connection.label: API request
connection.description: Public API traffic with trusted client network metadata.

steps.title: Forward requests to gateway instances
steps.content: Route each request to a healthy gateway. Correctness comes from the shared subject state, not from keeping all of a caller's requests on one gateway instance.

connection.label: Load-balanced API request
connection.description: Trusted ingress metadata accompanies the request; gateway affinity is not the rate-limit state mechanism.

steps.title: Make an atomic shared-state decision
steps.content: The gateway asks the authoritative Redis shard to atomically check and update the selected user or IP policy. Co-locate all state required for one subject decision where the datastore requires same-shard scripts; do not independently increment per-gateway counters and sum them later when the policy requires an exact decision.

connection.label: Atomic policy check and state update
connection.description: One authoritative per-subject decision updates compact shared Redis state and its algorithm-specific expiry.

steps.title: Resolve tier and algorithm policy
steps.content: Evaluate a local bounded cache of versioned tier policies on the request path; refresh snapshots asynchronously or from policy-change notifications. Define explicit behavior for a cache miss or stale version, and do not synchronously read the policy database for each request. Keep counters out of this configuration path.

connection.label: Versioned tier policy refresh
connection.description: Off-path policy snapshot refresh and change propagation; the gateway serves requests from its bounded local cache, while live per-request counters remain in shared Redis state.

steps.title: Forward admitted requests only
steps.content: After the limiter admits a request, the gateway forwards it to the protected business API. A deny decision terminates at the gateway and never consumes application capacity unnecessarily.

connection.label: Admitted API request
connection.description: Only requests that pass the applicable user/IP and tier policy reach business handling.

steps.title: Return a clear limit response
steps.content: For an over-limit request, return HTTP 429 with a stable error body and the applicable limit headers. Derive reset and retry guidance from the selected algorithm rather than promising a reset time that algorithm does not define.

connection.label: 429 response and rate-limit headers
connection.description: Stable error code/message plus RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, RateLimit-Reset, and Retry-After when applicable.

steps.title: Export aggregated breach telemetry
steps.content: Publish bounded metrics asynchronously so queue or analytics slowness does not add a synchronous dependency to the under-10ms overhead budget. Prefer aggregation over a separate event for every denied request at millions of requests per second.

connection.label: Batched breach and health metrics
connection.description: Asynchronous, privacy-safe telemetry; the request decision does not wait for analytics or alert delivery.

steps.title: Aggregate the operational stream
steps.content: Consume telemetry into bounded-cardinality views for breaches, latency, counter-store health, and policy freshness.

connection.label: Rate-limit telemetry stream
connection.description: Batched operational signals for aggregation and trend detection.

steps.title: Drive breach and health alerts
steps.content: Send aggregated operational findings to monitoring. Tune alert thresholds from observed traffic and incident history; do not infer thresholds from the problem statement.

connection.label: Breach and limiter-health signals
connection.description: Aggregated alert inputs without per-user or raw-IP metric labels.

steps.phase: Review algorithm, accuracy, and scale tradeoffs
steps.title: Select a default algorithm without hard-coding every tier
steps.content: Make the default explicit, but retain an algorithm selector in versioned policy so tiers can choose an algorithm that matches their burst and precision needs.

decision.question: Which algorithm should the gateway use by default while preserving support for other policy choices?
decision.chosen: Use token bucket as the default policy algorithm and select the algorithm per versioned tier policy.
decision.chosenReason: Token bucket state is compact, supports refill over time, and permits a configured burst while enforcing a sustained rate. A per-policy selector preserves the brief's requirement to support multiple algorithms.

alternatives.tradeoff: Simple and memory-efficient with a clear reset boundary, but a caller can concentrate traffic on opposite sides of a boundary.
Tracks events precisely within the moving window, but state grows with request volume and requires cleanup.
Uses less state than a per-request log and smooths fixed-window boundaries, but estimates traffic across adjacent windows.
Smooths output toward a steady rate; queueing can add latency, while a reject-on-full form trades smoothing for immediate denial.

properties.purpose: Validate JWT identity and trusted client metadata, resolve versioned tier policy from a bounded local policy cache, and apply the algorithm selected by that policy. Use token bucket as the default with compact shared Redis state and an atomic decision; retain fixed-window, sliding-window log/counter, and leaky-bucket implementations for policies whose boundary, precision, memory, or smoothing tradeoffs fit. Route only allowed calls to the application and return actionable HTTP 429 errors with applicable limit, remaining, reset, and retry guidance.

steps.phase: Review algorithm, accuracy, and scale tradeoffs
steps.title: Make window and reset behavior algorithm-specific
steps.content: A fixed window stores a count and window identity, then expires or resets that state at the boundary. A token bucket refills from elapsed time and reports when capacity is available rather than pretending to have a discrete reset. Sliding log and sliding counter have different precision and memory costs. Use atomic check-and-update on the authoritative Redis primary for each subject decision; hash-partition subjects to spread independent keys. If a globally exact quota must span regions, route a subject to one authoritative home or accept the latency/availability cost of coordination. Regional token allocations can reduce coordination but change utilization and consistency behavior; make that product choice explicit.

steps.phase: Review algorithm, accuracy, and scale tradeoffs
steps.title: Bound clock, cache, and failure behavior
steps.content: Use the authoritative datastore's time inside the atomic operation rather than gateway wall clocks, and observe clock drift across Redis primaries and failovers. Clamp backward elapsed time so clock corrections do not create negative refill; a primary clock jump still needs detection and an explicit recovery policy. Keep only versioned policy metadata in a bounded in-memory gateway cache; do not cache independent correctness counters there. Expire compact Redis algorithm state according to each policy, monitor key cardinality and memory pressure, and avoid silently evicting live counters. The brief does not decide fail-open versus fail-closed behavior when Redis is unavailable; define it per route risk, expose the degraded mode, and do not imply accurate enforcement while state is unreachable.

steps.phase: Review algorithm, accuracy, and scale tradeoffs
steps.title: Scale from measured request-path and hot-key pressure
steps.content: The brief calls for millions of requests per second and less than 10ms of rate-limit overhead; these are supplied requirements, not evidence that a particular deployment meets them. Measure gateway evaluation latency, Redis round trips, shard saturation, hot subjects/IPs, memory per active policy key, and denial telemetry lag. Scale gateway instances and Redis partitions from those observations. A single hot subject remains a serialization point for exact atomic counting; consider subject affinity or reserved regional budgets only after reviewing their latency, availability, utilization, and consistency tradeoffs.

scaleTrigger.metric: Gateway evaluation latency, Redis round trips and shard saturation, hot-subject concentration, active-key memory, and telemetry lag
scaleTrigger.action: Scale gateway capacity and repartition independent subjects; review hot-key ownership and any regional budget allocation against the required counting semantics
scaleTrigger.impact: Addresses observed throughput or state pressure while making any exactness, latency, or utilization tradeoff visible.
